title: Labour-Market Crack Flips Rate Outlook from Hike Risk to Cuts, Pulling Yields and Dollar Lower
content: Over the window the US rates narrative inverted. It opened with the Fed holding at 3.50-3.75% on 30 July amid firm inflation, three officials dissenting in favour of a hike and Chair Warsh hinting further tightening might be warranted, keeping the dollar bid and the curve heavy. The 1 August payrolls report shattered that framing: employment fell around 23,000, May and June were revised down by roughly 100,000 combined, and wage growth cooled to 3.2%. A tame July CPI on 12 August, headline 3.4% and core 2.5% year-on-year, reinforced the shift. Markets swung from pricing September hike risk towards holds and eventual cuts. UST yields fell, the 2-year towards 4.16% and the 10-year near 4.61%, and the dollar index slipped under 100, softening USD/JPY. Every subsequent data print became pivotal for cross-asset direction.

title: US Equities Melt Up to Fresh Records as AI Leadership and Easier-Policy Bets Broaden the Rally
content: US equities extended a powerful advance to successive all-time highs across the four weeks, with the S&P 500 closing above 7,700 and pushing beyond 7,800 for the first time. The move was propelled by the AI complex, megacap technology alongside infrastructure names such as CoreWeave and Super Micro, but broadened as the collapse in hike expectations removed a key headwind and softer oil eased cost pressures. Cooling inflation and lower yields lifted rate-sensitive sectors, while records in the Dow and Nasdaq signalled improving participation. The rally underscored how tightly equity sentiment remains bound to the policy path and to the durability of AI capital spending. With valuations stretched and index concentration high, positioning, breadth and the resilience of tech earnings stayed central, leaving indices exposed to any data that revives tightening fears.

title: Gold Powers to Record Highs on Softer Dollar, Central-Bank Demand and Fiscal Angst
content: Gold's structural bull run was a persistent cross-asset signal through the window, with bullion setting fresh records above $4,000 and printing near $4,070 in early August. A softening dollar, itself a product of the dovish rate repricing, made the metal cheaper for overseas buyers and amplified gains, while steady central-bank accumulation, elevated fiscal deficits and lingering questions over Fed independence under Chair Warsh underpinned demand. The advance persisted even as firm Treasury yields raised the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset, a tension analysts flagged as capping runaway upside. Gold's resilience alongside record equities and a weaker dollar reflected investors hedging currency debasement and policy-credibility risks rather than pure recession fear. The move reinforced gold's role as the market's preferred store-of-value hedge, keeping it sensitive to the dollar and the evolving rates path.
